title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
gist: Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were trivially guessable (all zeros except the final byte), so attackers can forge certificates trusted by unpatched roots; browsers blocked them via revocation lists, but the wider ecosystem is patching by removing the emSign ECC Root CA - G3. The incident exposes weaknesses in web PKI trust breadth, CAA and mTLS use, and links to post-quantum and shorter-lifespan certificate trends.

insights.claim: Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates (six TLS, two codesigning) were compromised, letting attackers forge certificates trusted by unpatched roots of trust.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Any unpatched system trusting these roots is exposed to MITM; track patch propagation.
insights.locator: Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate Certificate Authority

insights.claim: The eMudhra keys were not stolen in a breach but generated insecurely: they were all zero except the final byte (4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 or 237), so they can be enumerated and their public keys inferred.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Poor entropy in key generation, not intrusion, is the root cause; audit CA key-generation processes.
insights.locator: There’s no evidence that eMudhra was breached

insights.claim: The flaw was found by 'Wayne', who submitted a proof.zip bundle with the statement 'we have a problem here', and Dennis Jackson built a summary site for the incident.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Public root-store incident reports are the discovery channel for CA failures.

insights.claim: Browsers blocked the affected intermediate CAs quickly via background revocation blocklists, but most other software relying on web PKI has no mechanism to filter intermediate CAs.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Non-browser software is the soft underbelly of web PKI; expect lagging exposure there.
insights.locator: Browsers were able to block the affected intermediate CAs

insights.claim: Many projects removed the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their roots of trust, which causes collateral damage for all legitimate certificates from CAs chained to that root.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Legitimate eMudhra-chained certificate holders face breakage risk.
insights.locator: That removal is causing collateral damage

insights.claim: Fixes have shipped in ca-certificates packages for Arch, Debian, Gentoo, Fedora and Ubuntu and in Electron, Go, pip, Python certifi, rustls-webpki, Rust webpki-roots and uv, but systems that are unpatched or past end of life stay vulnerable.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Mozilla-derived cacert bundles propagate trust decisions across open source; watch for stale embedded bundles.
insights.locator: The ca-certificates packages in Arch, Debian

insights.claim: Applications that bundle their own cacerts file will keep trusting the compromised CAs, while platforms such as Dart 3.13 (August 2026), which no longer embeds a cacerts file, can pick up fixes via system roots.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Relying on system roots speeds remediation; bundled trust stores are a hidden liability.
insights.locator: Some languages and frameworks no longer bundle roots of trust

insights.claim: Using WebPKI CAs for mTLS client authentication is especially exposed because attackers can mint a certificate and authenticate to the endpoint without needing a BGP hijack or network attack.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Services that accept web PKI roots for client auth should be reviewed first.
insights.quote: The people who should be really scared right now are those using WebPKI CAs for mTLS / TLS client authentication.
insights.locator: Certificates are also used for authentication

insights.claim: DNS CAA records cannot stop forged certificates because a forger will not perform the check, and CAA uptake remains low even among popular sites.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: CAA is a control on honest CAs only; do not count on it against key compromise.

insights.claim: Wider use of Certificate Transparency outside browsers could let clients reject forged certificates that do not appear in logs, as RFC6962 and RFC9162 define, a goal Moxie Marlinspike's 2011 Convergence also pursued.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: CT enforcement in non-browser clients is a missing layer worth tracking.
insights.locator: Certificate Transparency also could have helped

insights.claim: The incident foreshadows the doomsday scenario raised by David Pollak of Spice Labs: popular CA root private keys being compromised, a serious concern as CAs remain anchored to classical RSA and ECC ahead of 'Q day'.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Post-quantum migration of CA roots is a long-run security spending driver.
insights.locator: This compromise foreshadows a doomsday scenario

insights.claim: Shorter certificate lifespans (47 days by 2029) make it easier to refresh certificates onto new anchors, and Let's Encrypt has proposed Merkle Tree Certificates as a lighter-weight, more containable alternative to post-quantum signatures such as ML-DSA-44.
insights.speaker: Chris Swan
insights.so_what: Certificate automation and MTC are the likely direction for web PKI resilience.
insights.locator: Certificate transparency and post quantum concerns come together
